orgContext: Logistics & customer operations · 312 employees · 7 departments · Kuala Lumpur, Penang, Johor

levels.meaning: Protect and use as a lever for the areas that need work.
Works today; monitor rather than intervene.
Inconsistent across the group. Candidate for workshop content.
Materially limiting the team. Design the intervention around this.

bands.name: Safety to speak
bands.question: Can I say what I actually think here?
bands.stake: When this is weak the company stops hearing about problems while they are still cheap to fix. Every other number becomes less trustworthy, including this survey.

bands.name: Ability to deliver
bands.question: Can I get my work done without fighting the organisation?
bands.stake: This is where wasted effort lives — rework, duplicated work, decisions that stall. It shows up in cost and in delivery dates before it shows up in attrition.

bands.name: Ability to absorb change
bands.question: When things go wrong or change, do we cope?
bands.stake: Predicts what happens to the company under pressure — a reorganisation, a lost client, a new system. Weak here means every change costs more than it should.

audiences.name: CEO / Managing Director
audiences.reads: The three perception bands and the direction of travel. Nothing below that.
audiences.decides: Which single constraint the company works on this quarter, and says so publicly. Approves the two actions that only a CEO can authorise.
audiences.neverSees: Individual records, department league tables used for ranking, or anything attributable to a person.

audiences.name: CHRO / Head of HR
audiences.reads: Priorities, perception gap, segments, and the human-review queue.
audiences.decides: Owns the board: assigns each action, holds the owner to the date, and publishes back to participants what changed.
audiences.neverSees: Transcripts. Only the trained reviewer opens a flagged session, and only the flagged one.

audiences.name: Department head
audiences.reads: Their own department against the organisation, and the perception gap between their view and their team's.
audiences.decides: The handover, decision-rights and consultation fixes inside their own department. The gap is theirs to close, not HR's.
audiences.neverSees: Other departments' detail, or any view that lets them identify who in their team said what.

audiences.name: Programme facilitator
audiences.reads: The Facilitator Intelligence Pack — evidence base, priority findings, anonymised voices, group composition.
audiences.decides: The programme design. Which blocks run, in what order, with which prompts.
audiences.neverSees: Named participants, or any data outside the engagement they are delivering.

audiences.name: Trained welfare reviewer
audiences.reads: Only sessions the pipeline flagged for welfare, safety or a named-individual disclosure.
audiences.decides: Escalation under the organisation's existing duty-of-care process.
audiences.neverSees: Aggregate dashboards. The review role is separated from the analytics role on purpose.

climateSpecs.name: Psychological safety
climateSpecs.pulseItem: In this team I can raise a mistake or disagree with a senior colleague without it being held against me.
climateSpecs.purpose: Can people ask questions, admit mistakes, challenge ideas and disagree with leaders without fear of penalty?

climateSpecs.name: Trust
climateSpecs.pulseItem: When colleagues in this team commit to something, I can rely on it being done.
climateSpecs.purpose: Do people believe colleagues and leaders keep commitments, act consistently and avoid unfair blame?

climateSpecs.name: Role clarity
climateSpecs.pulseItem: It is clear who owns each decision and each handover in the work I do.
climateSpecs.purpose: Do people know who decides, who owns each task, how handovers work and when to escalate?

climateSpecs.name: Goal alignment
climateSpecs.pulseItem: My department's targets pull in the same direction as the departments we depend on.
climateSpecs.purpose: Does the team share priorities and outcomes, including across departments?

climateSpecs.name: Collaboration
climateSpecs.pulseItem: Working across departments here is straightforward when I need something.
climateSpecs.purpose: Does the team coordinate, resolve dependencies and work across departments?

climateSpecs.name: Constructive conflict
climateSpecs.pulseItem: Disagreements in this team get discussed openly and resolved.
climateSpecs.purpose: Can people disagree openly, separate ideas from personalities and reach a workable decision?

climateSpecs.name: Leadership openness
climateSpecs.pulseItem: My manager invites input before deciding, and explains decisions afterwards.
climateSpecs.purpose: Do leaders listen, invite input, explain decisions and respond to concerns?

climateSpecs.name: Inclusion and belonging
climateSpecs.pulseItem: In team discussions, my contribution is heard and taken seriously.
climateSpecs.purpose: Do people feel respected, heard and able to contribute to decisions that affect them?

climateSpecs.name: Accountability
climateSpecs.pulseItem: In this team, agreed actions are followed through and reviewed.
climateSpecs.purpose: Does the team keep commitments, address underperformance and follow through?

climateSpecs.name: Collective resilience
climateSpecs.pulseItem: When priorities change suddenly, this team adapts without breaking down.
climateSpecs.purpose: Can the team adapt, re-prioritise and support each other through setbacks and pressure?

scenarios.title: Missed deadline
scenarios.setup: A colleague in another department has delayed a deliverable you depend on. Your own commitment to a customer is now at risk, and this is the second time it has happened.
scenarios.ask: What do you do next, and what exactly do you say to them?
scenarios.probe: And if the delay happens again the following week — what changes?

scenarios.title: Disagreement with a manager
scenarios.setup: Your manager has decided to bring a launch date forward. You believe the new date creates a real operational risk that senior management cannot see from where they sit.
scenarios.probe: Suppose the decision stands after you raise it. What do you do then?

scenarios.title: Departmental conflict
scenarios.setup: Two departments are blaming each other for a failed handover to a customer. You are in the meeting where it surfaces, and both sides are describing the same events differently.
scenarios.ask: How do you handle the conversation?
scenarios.probe: What would you put in place so it does not happen a third time?

scenarios.title: Overloaded colleague
scenarios.setup: A teammate tells you privately that they cannot complete their part of the work this week. Your own workload is already full, and the deadline is shared.
scenarios.ask: What do you say and what do you do?
scenarios.probe: What do you tell your manager, and when?

scenarios.title: Sudden change
scenarios.setup: Three days before delivery, the requirement changes materially. Half the work already done no longer applies, and the team is tired.
scenarios.ask: What are your first three moves?
scenarios.probe: How do you communicate it to the rest of the team?

interventions.trigger: People can explain their ideas, but they do not challenge decisions from above.
interventions.objective: Junior and mid-level staff raise a disagreement with a senior colleague in the room, and leaders demonstrably respond to it.
activities: Mistake-sharing protocol — leaders go first, naming a decision they got wrong
Speaking-up ladder: rehearse raising a concern at three levels of directness
Leader listening rounds — senior staff may only ask questions for 20 minutes
Anonymous-to-attributed exercise: team converts anonymous themes into owned statements
facilitatorPrompts: What would have to be true for you to disagree with your manager in a meeting?
Who in this room has changed a decision because someone junior pushed back?
What happens here to the person who raises the awkward thing?
observationChecklist: Who speaks first after a senior person states a position
Whether disagreement is addressed or deflected
Whether leaders ask questions or defend
Silence patterns by level and by department
managerActions: Leaders adopt a stated response protocol for challenge (acknowledge → explain → decide)
Each manager names one decision they will consult on before deciding
interventions.measure: Psychological safety index and the manager–staff gap on the same item at 30 and 60 days.
interventions.format: Half-day workshop, mixed-level tables, leaders present throughout

interventions.trigger: Trust is strong inside departments and weak across them; coordination fails at the handover.
interventions.objective: Each cross-department dependency has a named owner, an agreed handover standard and a shared measure.
activities: Dependency mapping — every department maps what it needs and what it owes
Handover simulation with a deliberately incomplete brief
Shared-customer-outcome challenge: mixed teams solve one end-to-end case
Handover standard drafting (what 'complete' means, per interface)
facilitatorPrompts: Walk me through the last request you sent to another department. What came back?
What does the other side wish you had included?
Which handover would you fix first if you could only fix one?
observationChecklist: Whether groups define the interface or defend their own function
Whether they design for the customer or for their department
Who volunteers to own a dependency
managerActions: Publish the dependency map and named owners within 14 days
Add one shared cross-department measure to the next quarter
interventions.measure: Collaboration and trust indices for cross-department items; count of escalations required.

interventions.trigger: Ownership of decisions and handovers is ambiguous; work stalls between roles.
interventions.objective: Decision rights, ownership and escalation paths are documented and tested against real stalled work.
activities: RACI workshop on three real pieces of work that stalled recently
Decision-rights mapping: which decisions need whom, and which do not
Escalation design — when, to whom, and how fast
Stall autopsy: replay one delayed deliverable and mark the boundary where it stopped
facilitatorPrompts: Who decided this? How did you find out?
What decision are you making that someone else should be making?
Where does work sit longest without an owner?
observationChecklist: Whether the group can name the decision-maker without debate
Whether escalation is described as a route or as a failure
Disagreement between levels on who owns what
managerActions: Publish a decision-rights table for the top ten recurring decisions
Set an escalation SLA and communicate it
interventions.measure: Role clarity index and stalled-work count reported at 30 and 60 days.
interventions.format: Half-day working session per department cluster

interventions.trigger: Disagreement is avoided rather than resolved; issues resurface as delays.
interventions.objective: The team has a shared protocol for disagreement and has used it on a live issue.
activities: Difficult-conversation role-play with the digital human, then with a peer
Disagreement protocol drafting (how we raise, how we decide, how we commit)
Live issue clinic: run one real unresolved disagreement through the protocol
facilitatorPrompts: What do you do when you disagree and the other person outranks you?
What is the disagreement nobody in this room is naming?
How do we know when a disagreement is closed?
observationChecklist: Whether disagreement is depersonalised
Whether the group converges or defers
Who withdraws when tension rises
managerActions: Adopt the disagreement protocol in the team's standing meeting
Review one previously avoided issue within 30 days
interventions.measure: Constructive conflict index; count of issues resolved at team level without escalation.

interventions.trigger: Agreed actions are not tracked to closure; follow-through depends on individuals.
interventions.objective: Every commitment made in the programme has an owner, a date and a review point.
activities: Commitment tracking: convert discussion into owned actions in the room
Peer accountability pairing across departments
Action ownership clinic — rewrite vague actions until they are testable
facilitatorPrompts: What happens here when an agreed action is not delivered?
Who will notice if this slips, and when?
What are we deciding to stop doing to make room for this?
observationChecklist: Whether actions get named owners without prompting
Whether dates are realistic or aspirational
Whether underperformance is addressed or absorbed
managerActions: Standing action review in the weekly management meeting
Publish action status to participants — closing the loop
interventions.measure: Accountability index; on-time closure rate of programme actions.
interventions.format: Integrated into every workshop close (45 minutes)

interventions.trigger: Under pressure the team fragments into individual coping rather than shared re-prioritisation.
interventions.objective: The team can re-prioritise together under time pressure and communicate the trade-off upward.
activities: Crisis simulation with a mid-exercise requirement change
Prioritisation challenge: more work than capacity, explicit trade-offs required
Workload communication drill — say no with a proposal
facilitatorPrompts: When the requirement changed, what did you stop doing?
Who told the customer, and when?
What would have helped most in the first hour?
observationChecklist: Whether the group re-plans or works harder
Whether trade-offs are named upward
Emotional regulation under time pressure
Who supports whom when the pressure lands
managerActions: Agree a re-prioritisation trigger and who can pull it
Review capacity assumptions with the executive committee
interventions.measure: Collective resilience index; stress-handling capability distribution.

interventions.trigger: Leaders rate openness highly while employees report that input rarely changes a decision.
interventions.objective: Leaders see the gap in their own data and commit to a visible change in how decisions are made.
activities: Facilitated dialogue on the anonymised employee themes
Leadership reflection: each leader states what they heard and what surprised them
Decision-consultation redesign for the three decisions employees named
facilitatorPrompts: Here is where your view and your team's view diverge most. What explains it?
When did input last change your decision, and did people know?
What will people see you do differently next month?
observationChecklist: Whether leaders explain or defend
Whether commitments are specific and observable
Whether employees present believe the commitment
managerActions: Each leader commits to one visible consultation change
Explain the reasoning for the next significant decision in writing
interventions.measure: Leadership openness index and the manager–staff perception gap at 30 and 60 days.
interventions.format: Executive session, then joint session with employee representatives

interventions.trigger: Departmental targets compete, so cooperation costs individuals their own measures.
interventions.objective: The conflicting measures are named and at least one shared outcome replaces or overrides them.
activities: Target-conflict mapping across departments
Shared-outcome design workshop
Trade-off negotiation: departments trade one measure each
facilitatorPrompts: Which of your targets makes it rational to say no to another department?
What would you have to give up for the end-to-end outcome to improve?
observationChecklist: Whether departments defend measures or the customer outcome
Whether executives resolve the conflict or leave it with the teams
managerActions: Executive committee resolves the named target conflicts
Publish the shared outcome and its owner
interventions.measure: Goal alignment index; cross-department escalation volume.

interventions.trigger: Airtime and influence concentrate in a subset of the team; others withdraw.
interventions.objective: Meeting practice changes so contribution is distributed and recorded.
activities: Airtime audit in a live meeting simulation
Round-robin and written-first meeting formats
Contribution mapping: who was heard, who was cited
facilitatorPrompts: Who has not spoken yet, and what do they think?
Whose idea was that originally?
observationChecklist: Airtime distribution by level, department and tenure
Interruption patterns
Whether contributions are attributed
managerActions: Adopt written-first for decision meetings
Rotate meeting facilitation
interventions.measure: Inclusion index; observed airtime distribution at the follow-up session.
interventions.format: Two-hour module inside a wider programme

interventions.trigger: Commitments are not reliably honoured, so people build private buffers and duplicate work.
interventions.objective: The team makes and keeps a small set of visible commitments to each other for 30 days.
activities: Reliability mapping: where do you build in a buffer, and why
Commitment contracting between dependent pairs
Blame-to-system reframing on two recent failures
facilitatorPrompts: Where do you add time because you cannot rely on the handover?
What promise could you make that the other side would actually feel?
observationChecklist: Whether failures are attributed to people or to the system
Whether commitments made are specific enough to fail visibly
managerActions: Review the commitment set at 30 days in public
Remove one structural cause of unreliability
interventions.measure: Trust index; buffer time reported by dependent teams.

priorities.finding: Trust is strong inside departments but weak across them; coordination breaks at the handover, not inside the team.
Departmental targets compete rather than combine, so cooperation costs individuals their own measures.
People can explain their ideas, but junior staff hold back from disagreeing with senior colleagues. The issue is upward communication and safety, not speaking ability.
Ownership of decisions and handovers is ambiguous, so work stalls at the boundary between roles rather than inside them.
Agreed actions are not tracked to closure, so follow-through depends on individual diligence.
Disagreement is worked through directly and separated from the personalities involved.
Input is sought before decisions and the reasoning is explained afterwards.
Commitments hold, information is shared, and people extend credit to each other by default.
Contribution is distributed and quieter members are actively brought in.
Pressure is met with shared re-prioritisation and mutual support.

suggestions.text: Protect the first thirty minutes of any change for re-planning
Make it normal to disagree in the room instead of afterwards
Make it clear who owns each handover
Give departments one shared measure for the customer outcome
Publish who decides what, so work stops sitting

voices.quote: It has been like this since the reorganisation, and most of us have simply adapted around it rather than fixing it.
People here will tell you in the corridor what they will not say in the room. My concern is that we lose the useful information.
The work sat for nine days because nobody knew who was supposed to sign off, and I only found out by asking three people.
In the meeting I could see the plan would not work, but I did not say anything because the decision had already come from above.
Inside my team it works well. The moment it crosses to another department, the request disappears and I have to chase.
I have a good relationship with my own team, but I do not know who to call in finance and I do not think they know me either.

voices.quote: People here will tell you in the corridor what they will not say in the room. My concern is that we lose the useful information.
It has been like this since the reorganisation, and most of us have simply adapted around it rather than fixing it.
Inside my team it works well. The moment it crosses to another department, the request disappears and I have to chase.
The work sat for nine days because nobody knew who was supposed to sign off, and I only found out by asking three people.
I have a good relationship with my own team, but I do not know who to call in finance and I do not think they know me either.
I build two extra days into every plan because I cannot rely on the handover arriving complete, and that has become normal.
In the meeting I could see the plan would not work, but I did not say anything because the decision had already come from above.
